entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18131"/><div sID="gen37361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18131"/>9. Translate, "As a widow (that is, of the ecclesiastical order of widowhood; a kind of female presbytery), let none be enrolled (in the catalogue) who is less than sixty years old." These were not deaconesses, who were chosen at a younger age (forty was the age fixed at the Council of Chalcedon), and who had virgins (in a later age called widows) as well as widows among them, but a band of widows set apart, though not yet formally and finally, to the service of God and the Church. Traces of such a class appear in <reference osisRef="Acts.9.41">Ac 9:41</reference>. Dorcas herself was such a one. As it was expedient (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6">Tit 1:6</reference>) that the presbyter or bishop should have been but once married, so also in her case. There is a transition here to a new subject. The reference here cannot be, as in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3">1Ti 5:3</reference>, to providing Church sustenance for them. For the restriction to widows above sixty would then be needless and harsh, since many widows might be in need of help at a much earlier age; as also the rule that the widow must not have been twice married, especially since he himself, below (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1Ti 5:14</reference>) enjoins the younger widows to marry again; as also that she must have brought up children. Moreover, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10">1Ti 5:10</reference> presupposes some competence, at least in past times, and so poor widows would be excluded, the very class requiring charity. Also, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.11">1Ti 5:11</reference> would then be senseless, for then their remarrying would be a benefit, not an injury, to the Church, as relieving it of the burden of their sustenance. Tertullian [On the Veiling of Virgins, 9], Hermas [Shepherd, 1.2], and Chrysostom [Homily, 31], mention such an order of ecclesiastical widowhood, each one not less than sixty years old, and resembling the presbyters in the respect paid to them, and in some of their duties; they ministered with sympathizing counsel to other widows and to orphans, a ministry to which their own experimental knowledge of the feelings and sufferings of the bereaved adapted them, and had a general supervision of their sex. Thus, this clause refers to <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">1Ti 5:19</reference>, as next clause, "neither be partaker of other men's sins," refers to <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">1Ti 5:20</reference>. Ellicott and Wiesinger understand it of receiving back into Church fellowship or absolution, by laying hands on those who had been "rebuked" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">1Ti 5:20</reference>) and then excommunicated (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.17">Mt 18:17</reference>); <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">1Ti 5:20</reference> favors this. This injunction to drink wine occasionally is a modification of the preceding "keep thyself pure." The presbyter and deacon were enjoined to be "not given to wine" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">1Ti 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8">8</reference>). Timothy seems to have had a tendency to undue ascetical strictness on this point (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1Ti 4:8</reference>; compare the Nazarene vow, <reference osisRef="Num.6.1-Num.6.4">Nu 6:1-4</reference>; John the Baptist, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.15">Lu 1:15</reference>; Ro 14). Paul therefore modifies the preceding words, "keep thyself pure," virtually saying, "Not that I mean to enjoin that kind of purity which consists in asceticism, nay, be no longer a water-drinker," that is, no longer drink only water, but use a little wine, as much as is needed for thy health. Alford thus: Timothy was of a feeble frame (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">1Co 16:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.11">11</reference>), and prone to timidity in his duties as overseer where vigorous action was needed; hence Paul exhorts him to take all proper means to raise his bodily condition above these infirmities.
